r: MTL 3600 asks elementary teacher candidates to examine video and written cases of children doing mathematics, using the Colorado K-6 content standards from an advanced perspective to build what the field calls mathematical knowledge for teaching. The applied task is diagnostic: inferring a specific child's reasoning strategy from evidence and deciding how to respond pedagogically, an interpretive activity task-exposure research treats as more resistant than routine computation, even though observed-usage data shows mathematical and computational categories are the most AI-used overall. AI can generate practice problems or explain a standard, but it does not perform the candidate's own diagnostic judgment about a particular learner's thinking. The binding constraint is dual: this course sits inside Colorado's board-approved elementary licensure curriculum, and it is explicit prerequisite scaffolding for five subsequent MTL content courses. At 24 months neither the diagnostic task nor the institutional architecture shows meaningful erosion.

By 2031, AI tutors will fluently generate worked examples, sample student errors, and explanations of the Colorado content standards, and observed-usage data already shows computer-and-mathematical tasks dominate AI use, so the raw content-delivery portion of this course is genuinely more automatable. What resists is the candidate's own diagnostic capacity: reading an actual child's written or video-recorded strategy and judging the underlying misconception, a jagged-frontier task where a plausible but wrong inference about a learner carries real instructional cost and is not obviously wrong to an untrained observer. The licensure curriculum and the foundational-scaffolding role for downstream number, algebra, geometry, and statistics courses do not relax on a single catalog cycle. The rating rises to Medium only if these constraints loosen; on this horizon they hold firm, so the instrumental case for the course remains largely Low, with content generation shifting but not replacing the diagnostic core.

A decade out, AI systems will plausibly analyze recorded classroom video and flag likely student misconceptions with real sophistication, meaningfully closing the gap between machine pattern-matching and candidate diagnosis; the base automatability factor rises accordingly. Even so, the course's dual anchors persist in the central case: Colorado's licensure-curriculum approval process for elementary preparation programs changes slowly, and MTL 3600 remains the prerequisite substrate on which five later mathematics-for-teaching courses depend, so foundational role and institutional lock-in jointly cap the erosion rather than eliminate it. The honest uncertainty is how much of the case-analysis work AI performs alongside the candidate versus how much diagnostic judgment the candidate must still exercise independently for licensure assessment. The rating moves to Medium, reflecting real but bounded erosion, not a confident prediction that the course becomes optional.
MTL 3600.d: This course approaches mathematical concepts outlined in Colorado Model Content Standard for Mathematics (grades K-6) from an advanced perspective. By examining video and written cases of children doing mathematics, students in this course will (1) connect their developing understanding of mathematics to the important mathematical concepts they will be required to teach; (2) turn their attention from understanding their own mathematical thinking, and the thinking of their classmates, to understanding the mathematical thinking of children; (3) lay the foundation for being able to learn mathematics from teaching.

r: MTL 3620 has secondary teacher candidates work through standards-based curriculum materials for grades 7 through 12, making explicit connections between the upper-division mathematics required for the major and the content those candidates will actually teach in school classrooms. The applied task is translational: taking rigorous mathematics and reconstructing it as accessible, standards-aligned instruction, which task-exposure research treats as more resistant than routine problem-solving even as observed-usage data shows mathematics-adjacent categories are heavily used for AI overall. AI can summarize a curriculum unit or generate lesson outlines, but it does not perform the candidate's judgment about how a specific mathematical idea should unfold for adolescent learners. The binding constraint is dual: the course is required within Colorado's board-approved secondary licensure curriculum, taken immediately before methods coursework, and it is prerequisite to the supervised field placement. At 24 months this translational task and the licensure architecture show little erosion.

By 2031, AI curriculum tools will draft standards-aligned unit plans and sample sequences for secondary mathematics competently, and observed-usage data continues to show heavy use in computer-and-mathematical categories, so the content-generation portion of the course is genuinely more exposed. What resists automation is the candidate's own judgment connecting advanced coursework to what a 7-12 classroom actually needs, a jagged-frontier task where a superficially reasonable curriculum sequence can miss adolescent misconceptions in ways that are not obvious without content-pedagogy training. The licensure requirement and this course's role feeding directly into the field-experience prerequisite chain do not loosen within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case shifts toward evaluating and adapting AI-drafted curriculum materials rather than producing them from scratch, but the rating stays Low at this horizon because the mandated sequence and its prerequisite function remain intact.

A decade out, AI systems will likely draft full secondary mathematics curriculum sequences with considerable sophistication, and the base automatability of the content-translation task rises meaningfully in the central case. Even so, Colorado's secondary licensure curriculum approval process is not expected to have removed this course from the required sequence, and MTL 3620 still functions as the direct prerequisite gateway into the field-experience course, so institutional lock-in caps the erosion rather than eliminating the requirement. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much curriculum-drafting work shifts to AI tools within the course itself versus how much candidates must still demonstrate independently for licensure and field placement. The rating moves to Medium to reflect that bounded erosion, not a confident forecast that translating mathematics into secondary curriculum becomes an AI-only task.
MTL 3620.d: This course, to be taken in the semester immediately prior to MTL 3630, approaches the mathematical concepts outlined in the Colorado Model Content Standards for Mathematics from an advanced perspective. The course uses standards-based curriculum materials as the focus for: (1) exploration of the central ideas of the mathematics curriculum in grades 7 through 12 and the connections among them, and (2) making explicit the connections between content covered in the mathematics courses required for the major and content taught in the school mathematics classrooms.

r: MTL 3638 places candidates in a secondary mathematics classroom for at least 80 hours under a mentor teacher, applying content knowledge from the major and MTL 3620 to live problems of practice with diverse learners, and directing a Secondary Mathematics Lesson Study as a mini teacher work sample. The applied work is embodied and real-time: reading a classroom in the moment, adjusting instruction to particular students, and building a mentoring relationship, activities task-exposure research places among the least automatable because they are interpersonal and psychomotor rather than informational. AI can help draft a lesson plan, but it cannot stand in front of adolescents and teach. The binding constraint is Colorado's teacher-preparation field-hour requirement, part of the roughly 800 clock hours secondary programs mandate, which a model cannot satisfy on a candidate's behalf. At 24 months the instrumental need for this supervised placement is fully intact.

By 2031, AI lesson-planning and formative-assessment tools will be more embedded in secondary classrooms, plausibly helping candidates draft the Lesson Study materials and analyze student work faster. That augments the placement; it does not substitute for the candidate physically leading a classroom of adolescents, responding to unplanned questions, and building the mentor relationship a field placement is designed to certify. Verification here is inseparable from presence — a mentor teacher must observe the candidate teaching to sign off on readiness, which no remote or AI-mediated proxy replaces. Colorado's field-hour requirement for secondary licensure does not relax on a catalog-cycle timescale. The instrumental case remains Low: AI changes what tools the candidate carries into the classroom, not whether the candidate must personally complete supervised, in-person teaching practice.

Over a decade, AI classroom-support tools could meaningfully change what a mentor teacher and candidate do together — surfacing real-time analytics on student engagement or automating parts of lesson documentation. But the specific competence MTL 3638 certifies is a human standing in front of secondary students, managing a live classroom of diverse learners, and demonstrating that capacity to a mentor teacher, which remains embodied, interpersonal work outside AI's substitutable range even under an aggressive capability trajectory. Colorado's clinical field-hour mandate for secondary licensure shows no credible path to elimination by 2036 in the central case. The rating holds Low; the genuine uncertainty is how much instructional support technology mediates the placement, not whether a candidate still needs supervised in-person teaching practice to earn licensure.
MTL 3638.d: Prospective teachers enrolled in this course will spend at least 80 hours with a mentor teacher in a secondary mathematics classroom. During this time, prospective teachers will apply the mathematical knowledge base developed in the mathematics major and in MTL 3620, and the framework for teaching developed in MTL 3630, to the problems of practice that arise in public-school classrooms of diverse learners. Prospective teachers in this course will direct a Secondary Mathematics Lesson Study, a mini teacher work sample.

r: MTL 3710 develops elementary teacher candidates' deep conceptual grasp of number and operations — pre-number concepts, place-value notation, decimals, scientific notation, and multiplicative reasoning — specifically for the purpose of teaching it, not merely computing it. The applied task is representational: choosing and interpreting multiple models of an operation so a child's partial understanding becomes visible, an interpretive skill task-exposure research treats as more resistant than the underlying arithmetic itself, even though observed-usage data shows computational and mathematical categories dominate AI use broadly. AI already executes the arithmetic instantly; it does not decide which representation exposes a particular misconception to a particular learner. The binding constraint is Colorado's board-approved elementary licensure curriculum, which requires this content-pedagogy sequence built on the MTL 3600 prerequisite. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this representational teaching knowledge is not eroded by AI's arithmetic fluency.

By 2031, AI systems will generate multiple representations of a number operation on demand and explain place-value or multiplicative reasoning fluently, and observed-usage data confirms mathematical tasks are among the heaviest AI-use categories, so the raw explanatory content is genuinely more exposed. What resists is the candidate's own judgment about which representation will surface a specific child's misconception in the moment, a diagnostic act where an AI-generated explanation that looks sound can miss the actual instructional target, echoing the jagged-frontier caution about mis-calibrated trust. Licensure-curriculum requirements do not restructure within a catalog cycle, and the course remains built on the mandated MTL 3600 foundation. The instrumental case shifts toward evaluating AI-generated representations rather than producing them, but the rating holds Low at this horizon because the mandate and the representational-judgment core persist.

A decade out, AI explanatory tools for elementary number concepts will likely be highly capable and widely available to candidates and children alike, and the base automatability of generating representations of an operation rises accordingly in the central case. Even so, Colorado's licensure curriculum is not expected to have dropped this required content course, and the candidate's diagnostic judgment about a child's specific numerical misconception remains a task an AI performs alongside, not instead of, the trained teacher. The honest uncertainty is how much explanatory content generation candidates offload to AI tools during the course itself versus how much representational judgment they must still demonstrate for licensure assessment. The rating moves to Medium, reflecting real erosion in content delivery bounded by institutional lock-in, not a confident claim the course becomes unnecessary.
MTL 3710.d: This course is an in-depth exploration of number and operations concepts that are relevant to elementary education. Topics will include pre-number concepts, place-value notation, decimals, scientific notation, basic number systems, interpretations and representations of numerical operations, and multiplicative reasoning.

r: MTL 3720 explores algebra concepts relevant to elementary education — algebraic axioms as generalizable properties of arithmetic, notation, equations and inequalities, functions, and modeling — with the applied purpose of teaching early algebraic reasoning rather than performing it. The task is pedagogical: helping candidates see how elementary arithmetic patterns generalize into algebra, and how to surface that generalization for children, an interpretive activity that resists automation more than the symbolic manipulation itself, even as observed-usage data shows mathematics is among the largest AI-use categories. AI solves equations instantly, but it does not decide how to introduce generalized arithmetic reasoning to an elementary learner encountering it for the first time. The binding constraint is Colorado's board-approved elementary licensure curriculum, built on the MTL 3600 prerequisite. At 24 months the instrumental need for this pedagogical-content competence is not eroded by AI's algebraic fluency.

By 2031, AI tools will fluently solve algebraic problems and generate explanations of how arithmetic patterns generalize, and observed-usage data continues to show mathematics-adjacent tasks are heavily used, so the raw content-explanation portion of the course is genuinely more exposed. What resists is the candidate's judgment about sequencing early algebraic ideas for elementary learners and recognizing when a child's informal reasoning is ready to generalize, a diagnostic task where a confident but poorly sequenced AI explanation can misdirect instruction in ways the jagged-frontier literature flags as a real verification risk. Licensure-curriculum requirements and the MTL 3600 prerequisite structure hold through a catalog cycle. The instrumental case shifts toward evaluating AI-generated pedagogical sequences rather than producing algebraic content from scratch, but the rating stays Low here because the mandate and diagnostic core persist.

A decade out, AI systems will likely generate sophisticated pedagogical sequences for introducing algebraic reasoning to elementary students, and the base automatability of this content-generation task rises meaningfully in the central case. Even so, Colorado's licensure curriculum is not expected to have removed this required course, and judging how a specific elementary learner is generalizing arithmetic into algebra remains a candidate competence an AI tool supports rather than replaces. The genuine uncertainty is how much sequencing work shifts to AI-assisted planning within the course versus how much pedagogical judgment candidates must still demonstrate independently for licensure. The rating moves to Medium to reflect that bounded erosion in content delivery, not a confident forecast that teaching elementary algebraic reasoning becomes an AI-only task.
MTL 3720.d: This course is an in-depth exploration of algebra concepts that are relevant to elementary education. Topics will include algebraic axioms as generalizable properties of elementary arithmetic, algebraic notation, equations and inequalities, functions, and algebraic modeling.

r: MTL 3730 covers geometry and measurement for elementary teaching: representing three-dimensional objects in two dimensions, composing and decomposing figures, congruence and similarity, standard and non-standard measurement, coordinates, transformations, and an introduction to axiomatic reasoning. The applied task is spatial-pedagogical: helping candidates reason about shape and space well enough to interpret a child's informal geometric thinking, which task-exposure research treats as closer to the protected critical-reasoning band than to routine computation, notwithstanding observed-usage data showing mathematics broadly is heavily AI-used. AI can describe transformations or generate proof sketches, but it does not perform the candidate's spatial reasoning or judge a child's non-standard measurement strategy. The binding constraint is Colorado's board-approved elementary licensure curriculum, built on the MTL 3600 prerequisite. At 24 months this spatial-reasoning and diagnostic competence is not meaningfully eroded by AI's geometric computation.

Licensure-curriculum requirements and the MTL 3600 prerequisite structure persist across a catalog cycle. The instrumental case shifts toward evaluating AI-generated geometric materials rather than producing them, but the rating holds Low here because the mandate and spatial-diagnostic core remain intact.

A decade out, AI systems with strong multimodal spatial reasoning could plausibly generate and even critique geometric arguments and measurement tasks at a level approaching classroom use, so the base automatability factor rises in the central case more than for a purely symbolic topic. MTL 3730.d: This course is an in-depth exploration of geometry and measurement concepts that are relevant to elementary education. Topics will include representation of 3-dimensional objects in two dimensions, composition and decomposition of geometric figures, congruence and similarity, standard and non-standard measurement, basic geometric figures and their properties, plane coordinates, transformations, and an introduction to axiomatic reasoning and proof.

r: MTL 3740 covers statistics and probability for elementary teaching — the nature and types of data, representations of data, basic probability, inference applied to educational research, an introduction to qualitative research, and assessment of student learning. The applied task is dual: interpreting data and research findings, which is squarely in AI's strongest observed-usage category, and then translating that interpretation into assessment judgments about actual children's learning, which is not. Task-exposure research finds programming- and data-adjacent tasks highly exposed, but the assessment-judgment component — deciding what a child's performance data means for instruction — carries real error cost and stays closer to the protected band. The binding constraint is Colorado's board-approved elementary licensure curriculum, built on the MTL 3600 prerequisite. At 24 months the data-analysis portion is already exposed, but the assessment-judgment core is not eroded.

By 2031, AI systems will routinely analyze classroom assessment data, generate probability visualizations, and summarize educational-research findings, directly extending the observed-usage pattern in which data and statistical tasks are among the most heavily used AI categories. That meaningfully erodes the raw analytical portion of this course. What persists is the candidate's judgment translating a statistical summary of student performance into an instructional decision — a jagged-frontier task where an AI-generated inference about learning can be technically correct yet pedagogically misapplied without expert oversight. Licensure-curriculum requirements and the MTL 3600 prerequisite structure do not relax within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case shifts toward verifying AI-generated data interpretations rather than computing them, but the rating holds Low at this horizon because the mandate and judgment core remain intact.

A decade out, AI data-analysis and probability tools will likely be deeply embedded in how educational assessment data gets summarized, and given how strongly data-adjacent work already skews toward AI use, the base automatability factor for this course's content rises substantially in the central case. Even so, Colorado's licensure curriculum is not expected to have dropped this required course, and the assessment-judgment competence — deciding what student data implies for instruction — remains a task candidates must demonstrate for licensure rather than delegate outright. The genuine uncertainty is how much statistical computation candidates offload to AI within the course versus how much interpretive judgment they still must exercise. The rating moves to Medium, reflecting substantial but bounded erosion, not a confident claim the course becomes unnecessary.
MTL 3740.d: This course is an exploration of basic concepts of statistics and probability that are relevant to elementary education, including the application of these concepts to the interpretation of educational research and the assessment of student learning. Topics will include the nature and use of data, types of data, representations of data, basic concepts of probability, conclusions and inference with a focus on educational research, an introduction to qualitative research, and assessment of student learning.

MTL 3850.d: This course serves as a STEM pedagogy seminar with a focus on conceptual development, conceptual change, collaborative learning, students' conceptions of various topics in mathematics and science, practical issues encountered in facilitating learning, managing the classroom, formative and summative assessment, and differentiating instruction in a collaborative environment.

Even projecting a decade of the kind of capability growth implied by rapidly lengthening AI task-time-horizons, the structural requirement that a licensure candidate complete a full-time, mentor-supervised classroom placement before certification is among the most durable constraints in the catalog. The work itself — managing a live secondary classroom, adjusting instruction in real time, being evaluated through lesson-study observation — is precisely the embodied, high-stakes, real-time interpersonal category that automation substitutes least readily, and Colorado's licensure architecture has no visible mechanism for converting clinical hours into simulated or AI-mediated equivalents within this horizon. The genuine uncertainty is what tools candidates use to prepare and document their teaching, not whether the placement is required. Confidence stays high and the rating holds Low, anchored jointly by embodiment and the licensure hard-brake.
MTL 4690.d: This course is a 16-week, full-time field experience with a skilled mathematics mentor teacher, supervised by an "MTL mentor," the official college supervisor, in an accredited secondary school. Prospective teachers who enroll in this course will, with the close and continual support of the mentor-teacher, take on increasing responsibility for, and learn from, all aspects of the work of a full- time mathematics teacher. Prospective teachers and their mentors will participate in two Secondary Mathematics Lesson Studies (which, together, constitute the teacher work sample), and in regular seminars conducted by the MTL mentor and other members of the Department of Mathematics and Statistics.

r: This upper-level seminar covers the intellectual and leadership work of an elementary mathematics specialist: equity and diversity in the classroom, cognitive-psychology and learning-theory foundations, mathematics-coaching and professional-development practice, the history of math education, and interpreting national and international assessment data. Interpreting standardized assessment results and synthesizing research literature on learning theory sit inside categories where observed-usage data shows Computer and Mathematical and writing-adjacent tasks heavily represented, and task-exposure research flags data-interpretation and writing-style work as positively associated with exposure. Coaching colleagues and leading equity-focused professional development remain more resistant, since they depend on situated judgment about a specific school community. No general-studies or GT-Pathways designation applies, but the course sits inside a sequenced elementary-math-specialist course of study built on several prerequisite MTL courses, giving it moderate programmatic weight. The rating is Low at 24 months.

By 2031, AI tools for summarizing assessment data, drafting professional-development materials, and surveying the research literature on mathematics learning will plausibly be routine for math specialists and coaches, extending the productivity gains professional-writing research already shows in faster drafting at comparable or higher quality. That shifts a meaningful share of this course's analytical and literature-synthesis content toward automatable territory, while coaching relationships, equity-sensitive classroom observation, and leadership judgment remain harder to substitute. Verification burden is moderate rather than low: an AI-drafted interpretation of assessment data or a coaching recommendation still needs a specialist's judgment before it reaches a school, given the jagged-frontier finding that unchecked AI use degrades accuracy outside its competence zone. The course sits in a defined specialist sequence but carries no hard clinical-hours mandate. The rating moves to Medium.

A decade of continued capability growth, in line with the fast task-time-horizon doubling trend, could plausibly make AI-assisted data interpretation, literature synthesis, and even first-draft professional-development design a default starting point for elementary math specialists, further compressing the analytical portion of this course's content. Coaching practice, equity leadership, and the interpersonal judgment involved in developing other teachers are more durable, since they depend on trust and situated context that automation does not replace. The course's programmatic role inside a sequenced specialist track provides a moderate, not hard, institutional anchor, so its footing is less secure than a licensure-clinical course over this horizon. Genuine uncertainty remains about how the specialist role itself gets redefined around AI-assisted analytics. Confidence is moderate given the description's breadth, and the rating holds at Medium rather than rising further.
MTL 4710.d: This course covers a variety of topics relevant to the role of an elementary mathematics specialist, including issues related to teaching such as equity and diversity, classroom environment, and basic ideas from cognitive psychology and learning theory. It will also cover issues related to mathematics education leadership, such as mathematics coaching, professional development, history of mathematics education, and the interpretation of data from national and international mathematics assessments.
